content: The initiation of breastfeeding, supplementation protocols, and rooming-in practices are essential components of postnatal care. Women should be informed about potential challenges they may face, such as breast engorgement or concerns about insufficient milk production, and provided with strategies to address these issues. Antenatal breastfeeding counseling should be personalized to meet the specific needs of the woman and her family, addressing their concerns and questions in a culturally and socially sensitive manner. Ideally, discussions about breastfeeding should begin during the first or second antenatal visit to allow sufficient time to address any challenges. This is particularly important in settings where women have limited antenatal visits or begin their care late in pregnancy. Women who deliver prematurely may miss opportunities to discuss breastfeeding if these conversations are delayed. Breastfeeding information should be provided in multiple formats, including printed or online materials in languages that mothers understand, even for those who are illiterate. However, not all women may read this information, and it may not address their specific questions. The information must be free from conflicts of interest, as stipulated by guidelines prohibiting companies that market infant and young child foods from providing education in health facilities. For women with special circumstances, such as adolescent pregnancies, high-risk pregnancies, or known congenital anomalies, discussions with knowledgeable providers should begin as early as possible to address the unique challenges of feeding a premature, low-birth-weight, or sick baby. Global standards recommend that antenatal discussions on breastfeeding include the importance of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, the risks of formula feeding, the significance of skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding initiation, rooming-in, proper positioning and attachment, and recognizing feeding cues. At least 80% of mothers receiving prenatal care should report having received breastfeeding counseling and be able to describe at least two of these topics. Immediate postnatal care should include uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and support for mothers to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth. Skin-to-skin contact facilitates the newborn’s natural rooting reflex, helps establish breastfeeding behavior, populates the newborn’s microbiome, and prevents hypothermia. Early suckling stimulates milk production and accelerates lactogenesis. Establishing a milk supply is critical, as many mothers stop breastfeeding early due to concerns about insufficient milk. Early breastfeeding initiation also reduces infant mortality risk. Skin-to-skin contact should begin immediately after delivery, regardless of the delivery method, and last for at least 60 minutes. Mothers should be supported in helping their baby attach and suckle at the breast. For mothers recovering from cesarean sections, skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding initiation can begin once the mother is alert and able to hold the infant. If medical instability delays breastfeeding initiation, mothers should still be supported to provide skin-to-skin contact and breastfeed as soon as they are able. Skin-to-skin contact is especially important for preterm and low-birth-weight infants, as it improves survival, thermal regulation, and breastfeeding initiation. Kangaroo mother care, involving prolonged skin-to-skin contact, should be the primary mode of care for stable preterm infants. Preterm infants can begin breastfeeding as early as 27 weeks of gestation if stable, but early and frequent milk expression is critical for stimulating milk production when direct breastfeeding is not yet possible. Postnatal breastfeeding support is essential, as even experienced mothers may face new challenges with a newborn. Counseling and support have been shown to increase breastfeeding rates up to six months of age. Early adjustments to positioning and attachment can prevent later breastfeeding problems, and frequent coaching builds maternal confidence. Practical support includes emotional encouragement, information sharing, and teaching concrete breastfeeding skills. First-time mothers and those with previous negative breastfeeding experiences require extra support. Mothers of preterm infants, twins, or those with health issues may need additional assistance to establish and maintain milk production. Facility staff should educate mothers on managing engorged breasts, ensuring a good milk supply, preventing sore nipples, and evaluating milk intake. Mothers should also be taught how to express breast milk to maintain lactation if separated from their infants. Supplementation with food or fluids other than breast milk should only occur when medically indicated, as it interferes with milk production and breastfeeding success. Newborns fed other foods or fluids may suckle less vigorously, leading to insufficient milk production and breastfeeding failure. Supplementation before facility discharge doubles the likelihood of breastfeeding cessation within six weeks. If supplementation is necessary, donor human milk is preferred, especially for low-birth-weight infants. If unavailable, breast-milk substitutes may be used temporarily. Mothers should be supported to express milk to maintain production and prioritize their own milk whenever possible. Rooming-in, where mothers and infants remain together 24 hours a day, is essential for responsive feeding and breastfeeding success. It allows mothers to recognize feeding cues and respond promptly, facilitating breastfeeding establishment. Separation should only occur for justified medical reasons. Mothers recovering from cesarean sections should have their infants nearby and receive practical support for breastfeeding. If infants require specialized care, efforts should be made to reunite mothers and infants or allow unrestricted visitation. Responsive feeding, also known as on-demand feeding, involves recognizing and responding to an infant’s hunger cues without restrictions on feeding frequency or duration. Mothers should be supported to practice responsive feeding as part of nurturing care, regardless of whether they breastfeed. Facility staff should help mothers recognize feeding cues and respond appropriately, even when separated from their infants for medical reasons. Mothers should be counseled on the use and risks of feeding bottles, teats, and pacifiers. While these items may be used when medically indicated, their use should not replace proper breastfeeding support. Pacifiers, if used excessively, may reduce the frequency of breastfeeding and maternal milk production. Mothers should be informed of these risks to make informed decisions.
